sm: Albert Mohler opens by returning to the scandal around Jensen Huang, which The Economist called unlike any other. NVIDIA's twelve member board unanimously reinstated Huang as CEO after meeting Sunday night, just days after saying it was not considering such a move. President Trump claimed credit, saying he was on the phone with the board. The board cited Huang's basic honesty and candor, which Mohler notes is not the same as upstanding character, given the affair with a woman now suspected of being a Chinese spy. NVIDIA lost about thirty percent of its value, then gained thirty-five percent after the announcement. Mohler calls this a Silicon Valley exception to the usual consequences of scandal.

Mohler asks why a president would intervene personally. He points to a possible personal relationship, but mainly to national security, since NVIDIA holds about ninety percent of the market for the most advanced chips and the United States wants to keep them from China. The administration has also negotiated a revenue sharing agreement with the company. Incoming House Speaker Hakeem Jeffries called the decision indefensible, irresponsible and incomprehensible and promised a wide investigation involving Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick. Mohler adds that many investors hold NVIDIA stock, that a Friday sell-off likely shaped the timing, and that the story will keep unfolding.

Mohler turns to the UN climate talks in Turkey, known as COP 31, which ended Sunday with no agreement. Headlines in the major papers described a collapse over a rift on fossil fuels. Europe and other nations insisted on language calling for a move away from fossil fuels, while other countries refused any explicit limit. Mohler lays out two arguments: one holds that global warming demands cutting fossil fuel use on a firm schedule, the other that no adequate substitute exists and billions depend on the energy grid for heat, electricity and health care. He notes that even the nations pushing the deal have not met their own goals. He calls the United Nations an oxymoron that many nations ignore. Speaking from a Christian worldview, he says global warming is a real threat but that cost-benefit analysis and human flourishing must guide a longer energy transition.

Mohler brings a Christian worldview to a more sentimental story, the death of Fiona the hippo at the Cincinnati Zoo after she ate a knit hat thrown into her enclosure. Fiona was born prematurely, survived against the odds, and became beloved around the world, prompting more than a hundred thousand expressions of grief. He sees this as a reflection of the image of God, with humans feeling a connection to other creatures, as in Adam naming the animals. He then turns to the fall, noting that hippos kill about five hundred people a year, and walks through a list of deadly animals, including crocodiles, snakes, snails, humans and mosquitoes, the deadliest at about a million deaths a year. He closes by saying such evidence of sin points to Christ's coming kingdom, when the lion and lamb will lie together.
sg: UN climate talks collapse over fossil fuels
